overview: Pictish communities and kingdoms occupied parts of early medieval Scotland. Their history survives in carved stones, workshops, food remains and outside accounts. The evidence reveals connected regional societies, not a single unchanged state. Political authority and language changed as Alba emerged, without a securely established single date when all Picts disappeared.

periods.title: Rhynie and regional centres
periods.summary: At Rhynie, enclosed timber settlements, imported vessels and metalworking debris document an important fifth- and sixth-century centre. These archaeological dates describe the site, not the founding of all Pictish kingdoms.

periods.title: Monasteries, workshops and learning
periods.summary: Portmahomack combined craft production with a cemetery and engineered water supply. Bede also records a Pictish king seeking Easter calculations and stone builders from Northumbria.

periods.title: Rebuilding after destruction
periods.summary: Portmahomack suffered burning around 800, followed by renewed craft activity and farming. The local destruction did not terminate every Pictish kingdom.

periods.title: Changing authority and the emergence of Alba
periods.summary: Fortriu ceased to appear in contemporary documents in the early tenth century. Alba's influence in the Highlands was uneven, with uncertain and changing frontiers.

items.text: Written references to Picts begin in the late third century. This first surviving name is not a secure founding date for a people or kingdom.
Fortriu, a powerful kingdom by the seventh century, is now located around the Moray Firth. Its full extent and relationship with smaller regions remain debated.

Rhynie's fifth- and sixth-century settlement had successive ditches and a larger timber palisade. The Craw Stane stood near an entrance. These excavated relationships connect symbol stones with an inhabited, repeatedly remodelled place.
An iron axe-shaped pin from Rhynie resembles the axe on the Rhynie Man stone. Clay moulds for comparable pins establish local manufacture, linking a carved image to the work of metalworkers.

Rhynie's ditch deposits contained imported amphora fragments, continental glass, crucibles and metalworking tools. The vessels demonstrate exchange connections, while production debris shows that the settlement also made valuable objects.

Around 700, Portmahomack's workers carved stone, worked metal and glass, and processed hides interpreted as parchment production. Combined with its burial pattern and infrastructure, this supports identification as a monastery.

Cattle bones dominate Portmahomack's animal remains. The researchers connect cattle with food, possible dairying and hides for parchment. Supporting a religious community required husbandry and skilled processing as well as prayer.

After the monastic phase, a Portmahomack workshop became a kiln barn with an upper floor and flue. Its alteration, together with grain remains, makes a change in everyday work visible in the buildings.

Charred barley and evidence for oats and wheat at Lairg document cultivation from about 450 onward. Such environmental traces reveal food production even where early medieval houses are difficult to identify.
The Hilton of Cadboll cross-slab, erected around 800, places a woman prominently in a hunting scene. The original was later cut and reused as a grave marker; the stone at the site today is a replica.

Bede reports that King Naiton asked Ceolfrid for guidance on Easter and builders for a stone church. His account shows royal interest in religious calculation and imported expertise, although it presents these exchanges through Bede's Christian viewpoint.

Burning and broken sculpture mark Portmahomack's destruction around 800. A Viking raid is a proposed explanation, not an identified attacker. Workers subsequently cleared debris and resumed metal and glass production.

ending.text: Pictish power centres shifted during the later ninth century, and Alba extended uneven authority into the Highlands in the tenth. This was a prolonged political and cultural transformation. The evidence does not support one conquest date or the disappearance of an entire population.

sources.title: Scottish Archaeological Research Framework, Highland Early Medieval: Introduction
sources.note: Paragraphs on earliest references, Fortriu, later ninth-century power shifts, Alba and undeciphered symbols. Frontiers and political control remain uncertain.

sources.title: Susan Kruse, Portmahomack: The Tarbat Discovery Programme
sources.note: Periods 1-3, especially the paragraphs beginning Around AD 700, Around AD 800 and Shortly after the raid. Monastery and attacker identifications are interpretations.

sources.title: Scottish Archaeological Research Framework, Farming, Fishing and Hunter Gathering
sources.note: Cultivated Food: Lairg and Portmahomack; Domesticated Animals: Portmahomack. Grain remains, kiln conversion and cattle use are site-specific evidence.

sources.title: AOC Archaeology, An Early Medieval Enclosure at Rhynie, Aberdeenshire
sources.note: 2017 excavation account: fifth- and sixth-century enclosure sequence, ditch deposits, imported amphorae and glass, axe pin and clay moulds. Imports do not identify the people transporting them.

sources.title: Historic Environment Scotland, Hilton of Cadboll Chapel
sources.note: Overview: cross-slab erected about 800, hunting scene with central woman, later reworking and distinction between the original and the replica.

sources.title: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of England, translated by A. M. Sellar
sources.note: Book II chapters 3 and 5 for Mellitus, Sabert and London; book V chapter 21 for Naiton, Ceolfrid, Easter and stone builders. Bede writes from a Christian ecclesiastical perspective.
